featured_reviews.review_text:
A Doctor Who Made Our Dreams Come True

My husband and I had been trying to conceive naturally for over two years without success. When we turned to Dr. Nikita for help with IVF, we immediately felt we were in the right hands.

In January, she recommended some tests to understand our situation better. The results weren’t great—my AMH was less than 0.5, and my FSH was low. Despite this, Dr. Nikita stayed positive and encouraged us to move forward. In our first cycle, we only got one egg. Rather than letting the cycle go to waste, we tried IUI, but unfortunately, it didn’t work.

In February, I developed a cyst, and Dr. Nikita suggested a hysteroscopy to ensure everything was on track. Her thoroughness reassured us that she was doing everything possible to help us. By March, we started another round of injections, and this time, we retrieved four eggs. Out of those, only one was of good quality, but it developed into a grade-one embryo.

Dr. Nikita’s experience and instincts were incredible. She believed my uterus lining was perfect for implantation in the same cycle, and we trusted her advice. The result? A positive pregnancy and now a healthy baby girl!

Throughout this journey, Dr. Nikita’s calm approach, expertise, and support made all the difference. Even when the odds were against us and donor eggs were considered, she gave us hope and helped us achieve our dream.

We’re forever grateful to Dr. Nikita for making parenthood possible for us. If you’re struggling with fertility, I can’t recommend her enough—she truly works miracles!

Choosing the right IVF clinic is one of the most important decisions in your fertility journey. The right center not only offers advanced treatments but also provides transparency, trust, and personalised care at every step.

When Should You Consult a Fertility Specialist?

Many couples try to conceive naturally for months or even years before seeking medical advice. However, certain signs may indicate that it is the right time to consult a fertility specialist for proper evaluation and guidance.

One of the most common signs is trying for pregnancy for a long time without success. If a couple has been trying to conceive for over a year without results, or for six months if the woman is above 35, it may be time to seek medical support. Early consultation can help identify underlying causes and avoid delays in treatment.

Irregular menstrual cycles are another important indicator. Conditions such as hormonal imbalance or polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) can affect ovulation and reduce the chances of natural conception. A specialist can assess these issues and recommend appropriate care.

Male fertility factors are also an important part of fertility evaluation. Low sperm count, poor motility, or other sperm-related concerns can affect conception. Foods to Avoid During IVF Treatment

Nutrition plays an important role during fertility care. While there is no strict “IVF diet,” certain foods are better avoided to support better outcomes and overall health during treatment.

Highly processed foods such as packaged snacks, fried items, and fast food should be limited. These foods are often high in trans fats, refined sugar, and preservatives that may affect hormonal balance. Excess sugar intake can also impact insulin levels, which is especially important for women with PCOS.

It is advisable to reduce caffeine consumption from coffee, energy drinks, and certain soft drinks. High caffeine intake may affect implantation in some cases. Alcohol should also be avoided during fertility treatment, as it can interfere with hormonal regulation and egg quality.

Raw or undercooked foods, including unpasteurised dairy, raw eggs, or uncooked seafood, should be avoided to reduce the risk of infection.

 High-mercury fish such as shark or swordfish are also not recommended. Maintaining a balanced diet supports the body during IVF, IUI, ICSI Treatments and helps create a healthier environment for conception.

Separating Truth from Myths About IVF

IVF is one of the most effective fertility treatments today, yet many myths create confusion and unnecessary fear. Understanding the facts helps couples take timely and confident decisions.

A common myth is that IVF always guarantees pregnancy. The fact is that IVF improves the chances of conception, but success depends on factors such as age, egg quality, sperm health, and overall medical condition. 

Another misconception is that IVF is extremely painful. In reality, most procedures are well-managed with modern techniques and patient-focused care, making them comfortable and safe.

Many believe IVF is only meant for women with severe fertility problems. In truth, IVF is advised for multiple conditions, including male infertility, blocked fallopian tubes, endometriosis, repeated miscarriages, and unexplained infertility. 

There is also a belief that IVF always results in twins or triplets. With careful embryo selection and transfer, the risk of multiple pregnancy is controlled.

Egg retrieval is one of the most important steps in the IVF process. It is a carefully planned medical procedure where mature eggs are collected from the ovaries so they can be fertilised in a laboratory. Understanding this step helps reduce fear and builds confidence before starting treatment.

Before egg retrieval, the ovaries are stimulated using fertility medications to help multiple eggs mature at the same time. During this phase, ultrasound scans and blood tests are done regularly to monitor follicle growth and hormone levels. Once the eggs (follicles) are ready, ovum pick-up (OPU) is timed very precisely after the trigger injection.

Why 12 eggs?

Because fertility works on probability. During egg freezing and IVF, eggs go through thawing, fertilisation (ICSI), embryo development, and genetic screening. At every stage, natural biological attrition occurs. This is normal reproductive physiology, not pessimism.

Twelve mature eggs is often used as a medically grounded planning benchmark in egg freezing, designed to account for natural loss and improve the probability of achieving at least one future live birth, depending on age and ovarian reserve.

"When it comes to fertility, sperm health matters more than most people realise. Nearly 40–50% of fertility challenges involve the male partner, yet male fertility testing is often delayed or overlooked.

It’s not just about sperm count. A complete semen analysis looks at motility (movement), morphology (shape), and sperm DNA integrity — all of which directly impact fertilisation, embryo development, and IVF outcomes.

Testing both partners early helps identify the real cause sooner, reduces unnecessary delays, and allows fertility specialists to plan treatment more accurately from the start.

"Diabetes & Fertility: What Most People Don’t Know

Having diabetes doesn’t mean you can’t conceive. It means your fertility journey needs the right preparation. 🌻💛

Uncontrolled blood sugar levels can impact fertility in both men and women:

• Women: irregular ovulation, cycle disturbances, egg quality issues, and higher PCOS risk
• Men: reduced sperm count, poor motility, and increased sperm DNA fragmentation

What’s often missed is this: better glucose control is directly linked to better fertility outcomes for both partners.

Before trying to conceive, it helps to:
🌻 Optimise blood sugar levels and HbA1c (as advised by your doctor)
🌻 Consult both an endocrinologist and a fertility specialist
🌻 Review medications, nutrition, and lifestyle factors that affect reproductive health

Technology can play a big role too. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM), insulin pumps, and fertility tracking tools now allow safer, more predictable conception planning.

In India, early-onset diabetes and high-carbohydrate diets mean fertility is affected earlier than many expect. That’s why early fertility screening and pre-conception planning matter.

FREEZING YOUR EGGS IN YOUR 30s

Fertility planning is becoming an important topic for many women, but decisions around egg freezing are often influenced by trends, online information, and individual circumstances.

Some important considerations include:

• Fertility potential may change with age
• Egg number and egg quality are both important factors in fertility discussions
• Conditions such as PCOS and Endometriosis can affect fertility experiences differently from person to person
• Previous ovarian procedures or medical history may be relevant in fertility planning
• Egg freezing is one option that may be considered as part of a broader fertility strategy

For some women, fertility preservation may be an option worth discussing. For others, timing and individual circumstances may differ.

Factors that may be considered include:

• age
• ovarian reserve assessment
• family planning goals
• relationship timelines
• medical history
• emotional and financial considerations

The focus should be on informed decision-making and understanding available options.

If you are considering fertility preservation, a discussion may include realistic expectations, fertility planning, and individualized guidance.

— Dr. Latika Chawla
Gynecological Endoscopic & Endometriosis Surgeon

Pelvic pain in Endometriosis can sometimes involve more than active disease alone.

For some women, ongoing discomfort may be influenced by multiple factors, including inflammation, tissue changes, muscle tension, movement patterns, and how the nervous system processes pain signals over time.

Adhesions are bands of scar tissue that may develop after inflammation, surgery, or disease processes. In some cases, they may affect how tissues and organs move in relation to one another.

Some women may experience symptoms such as:

• pelvic discomfort
• stiffness or restricted movement
• muscle tension
• increased sensitivity to pain
• reduced confidence with movement due to discomfort

Every experience can be different, and symptoms do not always correlate directly with the amount of visible disease.

This is one reason why endometriosis care often extends beyond treatment of disease alone and may also focus on overall function, movement, symptom management, and quality of life.

If pelvic symptoms continue after treatment or surgery, discussing them with your healthcare professional may help guide further evaluation.

📍 Andheri West | Juhu | Surya Hospital (Santacruz) | Lilavati Hospital (Bandra)
— Dr. Latika Chawla
Gynecological Endoscopic Surgeon & Endometriosis Surgeon

Can having fewer periods extend fertility?

There has been recent discussion around fertility research and whether changes in menstrual patterns could one day influence reproductive aging.

Here’s the important context:

• Women are born with a finite ovarian reserve
• Fertility is influenced by several factors, including age, egg quality, hormones, genetics, and overall ovarian health
• Current evidence does not support reducing menstrual frequency as an established way to preserve fertility
• Research in this area is ongoing and is not part of routine fertility care today

An important question researchers continue to study is:

Can aspects of reproductive aging eventually be better understood or influenced in the future?

At present, there is no established treatment shown to extend fertility lifespan simply by reducing periods.

It is also important to remember that menstrual health, ovulation, hormone balance, and overall wellbeing are interconnected.

For women with:
• fertility concerns
• ovarian cysts
• endometriosis
• low AMH
• delayed family planning considerations

an individualized discussion and fertility assessment may help guide informed decisions.

Science continues to evolve, but healthcare decisions are best made using evidence-based information and personalized medical guidance.

— Dr. Latika Chawla
Gynecological Endoscopic & Endometriosis Surgeon

📍 Andheri West | Juhu | Surya Hospital (Santacruz) | Lilavati Hospital (Bandra)

Some exercises may feel different when living with Adenomyosis

Exercise is often encouraged for overall health and wellbeing, but every woman’s experience with Adenomyosis can be different.

Some women report that certain activities may be associated with symptoms such as:
• bloating
• pelvic heaviness
• cramps
• fatigue
• increased discomfort during flare phases

This does not mean exercise is harmful. Factors such as symptom patterns, pelvic floor tension, inflammation, and individual comfort levels may influence how the body responds.

During symptomatic phases, some women may find gentler activities more comfortable, such as:
• walking
• mobility exercises
• restorative yoga
• breathing practices
• guided pelvic health exercises

Movement is not one-size-fits-all, and what feels supportive can vary from person to person.

If pelvic symptoms are affecting your daily life or exercise routine, speaking with a healthcare professional may help guide the next steps.

— Dr. Latika Chawla
Consultant Gynecologist & Endometriosis Surgeon

Many women experience painful or heavy periods and assume it is a normal part of life.

Sometimes, these symptoms may be linked to conditions like adenomyosis, which can often go unrecognized in the early stages.

Symptoms such as increasing menstrual pain, heavy bleeding, pelvic discomfort, or a feeling of heaviness should not be ignored.

A timely gynecological evaluation can help identify the possible cause and guide women toward appropriate management options based on their individual health needs.

If your symptoms are affecting your daily life, consider consulting a qualified specialist for proper assessment.

— Dr. Latika Chawla
Gynecological Endoscopic & Endometriosis Surgeon

📍 Andheri West | Juhu | Surya Hospital (Santacruz) | Lilavati Hospital (Bandra)

PCOS is often misunderstood.

And now, many experts are reconsidering the name itself.

Why?

Because “Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome” does not fully explain what many women actually experience.

Many women with PCOS may not even have ovarian cysts. Instead, they struggle with:
• irregular periods
• acne and hair growth
• weight fluctuations
• insulin resistance
• fatigue
• fertility concerns

This is why the term PMOS (PolyMetabolic Ovarian Syndrome) is entering medical conversations.

The condition is not just about the ovaries. It is closely linked to metabolism, hormones, inflammation, and long-term health.

Early diagnosis and structured treatment can make a significant difference.

If you are experiencing persistent cycle irregularities or hormonal symptoms, do not ignore them.

— Dr. Latika Chawla
Consultant Gynecologist & Endometriosis Surgeon

Are GLP-1 medications like Ozempic affecting your periods or fertility?

GLP-1 medications (such as Ozempic and Mounjaro) are increasingly used for weight management and metabolic health. Some women may notice changes in their menstrual cycle or ovulation patterns after starting these treatments.

Here’s what is commonly observed:

• Improved insulin sensitivity may support more regular cycles in some women with PCOS
• Ovulation may resume, which can increase the chance of natural conception
• Absorption of oral contraceptive pills may vary, especially during dose adjustments
• These medications support metabolic health but are not a cure for PCOS
• They are not recommended during pregnancy and should be used under medical guidance

Every individual responds differently.

If you’ve noticed changes in your cycle after starting GLP-1 therapy, it’s important to discuss this with a qualified specialist.


— Dr. Latika Chawla
Gynecological Endoscopic & Endometriosis Surgeon

featured_reviews.review_text:
Our journey toward parenthood was not an easy one and like many couples in Mumbai, we found ourselves surrounded by countless IVF and fertility centres almost one in every locality. However, what truly distinguishes Ankoor Fertility Clinic from the rest is that, unlike many clinics that often feel driven primarily by commercial motives, this institution is driven by passion, integrity and genuine care for patients.

Before visiting Ankoor, my wife and I had already consulted two other gynecologists. Our previous experiences felt largely procedural, where treatments seemed to follow a fixed medical playbook with little effort to understand us as individuals. Meeting Dr. Kedar Ganla was a completely different experience altogether.

What impressed us most was his extraordinary dedication and depth of involvement in understanding every aspect of our lives not just our medical reports. He carefully studied our medical history, lifestyle, dietary habits, stress levels, routines and even patterns that we ourselves had overlooked. His approach was deeply analytical yet profoundly humane.

In many other fertility centres, we felt IVF would have been immediately recommended as the default solution. However, Dr. Kedar Ganla was remarkably honest with us. He explained that even if IVF were attempted immediately, the chances of success would remain low unless we first addressed certain health and lifestyle concerns. More importantly, he reassured us that, in his professional opinion, we did not necessarily require IVF at all. He believed that with disciplined lifestyle changes, proper diet, exercise, weight management, and medication, natural conception was genuinely possible for us.

He gave us clear health goals and monitored our progress rigorously during every consultation. In fact, he often reminded us like a strict yet caring school headmaster about the importance of discipline and consistency. At times he even scolded us for not following instructions properly, but today we realise that his firmness came from sincere concern and commitment toward our success. Sometimes, especially in one’s mid and late thirties, that kind of accountability becomes necessary.

The day we discovered that we had conceived naturally was one of the happiest and most emotional moments of our lives. We immediately remembered Dr. Kedar’s words when he confidently told us, “You will be able to conceive naturally.” and indeed, we did.

That, however, was only the first milestone of our pregnancy journey. There were additional complications and concerns during the pregnancy, many of which we may not fully understand technically even today by us. But throughout the entire journey, we placed complete trust in Dr. Kedar Ganla and Dr. Manjusha Ganla. They, along with their entire team, stood firmly beside us not only until delivery, but even during the post-pregnancy phase with unwavering support and care.

This review is not written for promotion, nor is it generated artificially. It comes from genuine gratitude and heartfelt appreciation. We simply wish to recommend and endorse doctor who practise medicine not merely as a profession, but as a passion and a responsibility toward human life.

We will always remain thankful to Dr. Kedar Ganla, Dr. Manjusha Ganla and the entire team at Ankoor Fertility Clinic for helping us achieve one of the greatest blessings of our lives.

Male fertility is often overlooked until the journey to parenthood takes longer than expected.

Advanced techniques like Microfluidics help select healthier moving sperm during IVF treatment, supporting a more personalised approach to fertility care.
This Men's Health Month, let's encourage earlier conversations, timely evaluations, and greater awareness around male fertility health.

A diagnosis of azoospermia can feel overwhelming, especially when a semen analysis shows no sperm. For many men, it may seem like the end of the road to fatherhood.

However, in some cases, sperm may still be present within the testes and can sometimes be retrieved through specialised procedures such as TESA, TESE or Micro-TESE. These retrieved sperm may then be used in IVF/ICSI treatment, offering some couples an opportunity to pursue pregnancy using their own sperm and eggs.
This Men’s Health Month, let’s remember that the right diagnosis and expert evaluation can make all the difference.

Dr. PGL Lalit Kumar, Head of Embryology and Scientific Director, Nova IVF Fertility

At Nova IVF Fertility, we guide you towards simple, sustainable habits that work with your lifestyle, helping you move forward, one step at a time.

Around 15–20 eggs begin developing in your ovaries each month.

But the body naturally selects just one dominant egg and asks the rest to stop growing.
This is a normal biological process, not a limitation.
In IVF, this process is supported differently, allowing multiple eggs to continue developing for better chances of conception.
